questions.question: Your team wants Copilot cloud agent to fix recurring lint failures from CI. Which task definition best matches GitHub's guidance for integrating an agent into the SDLC?

options.text: 'Fix the lint errors and merge to main when CI is green.'
'Given a failing CI run ID and the file paths it reports, modify only those files so that `npm run lint` exits 0 locally and in CI, and open a draft PR with the changes.'
'Improve code quality across the repo.'
'Refactor the project to remove all lint warnings forever.'

questions.explanation: Agents need explicit inputs (failing CI run ID, file paths), explicit outputs (modified files, draft PR), and verifiable success criteria (`npm run lint` exits 0). A allows the agent to merge without human review, which violates the contributor model and PR governance. C and D are unbounded goals with no measurable definition of done.

questions.question: Which of the following are anti-patterns when integrating agents into the SDLC according to GitHub's guidance? (Select 3.)

options.text: Allowing the agent to merge its own pull requests
Defining success criteria as automated checks the agent must satisfy
Skipping CODEOWNERS review on agent-authored PRs
Treating agent output as 'final' rather than as a contribution
Posting an inspectable plan to the PR before code changes

questions.explanation: A: cloud agent is already restricted from merging PRs, and overriding that defeats supervision. C: bypassing CODEOWNERS removes the human review gate. D: violates the contributor model. B and E are recommended practices: measurable success criteria and an inspectable plan posted before action.

questions.question: Place the following SDLC integration steps in the recommended order when onboarding a new agent for an existing repository.

options.text: Define success criteria as automated checks
Enumerate the discrete steps the agent must perform
Configure branch protection and CODEOWNERS for the target paths
Assign a scoped issue to the agent and review its draft PR
Document inputs and outputs for the agent task

questions.explanation: GitHub's contributor model first decomposes the task (steps, inputs/outputs, success criteria), then enforces governance (rulesets, CODEOWNERS), and only then assigns work. Reviewing the draft PR is the closing loop.

questions.question:
[Case study context] Contoso wants to introduce Copilot cloud agent on a payments service. The service has a strict release process with manual approval gates. The platform team must ensure agents fit the existing SDLC without weakening release controls.

Which framing of the agent's task is most aligned with GitHub's contributor model?

options.text: Give the agent maintainer access so it can self-merge after running tests
Define the agent's job as 'open a draft PR with code and tests that satisfy the acceptance checks defined in the issue'
Allow the agent to push directly to the release branch when CI is green
Configure the agent to bypass branch protection on payments/*

questions.explanation: Draft PR with verifiable acceptance checks is the canonical contributor-model framing. A, C, D all remove the human review gate the existing release process depends on.

Which controls should the platform team keep in place to preserve release-process integrity? (Select 2.)

Disable session logs to reduce audit noise
Require CODEOWNERS review on payments/*
Grant the agent the workflow scope so it can dispatch deployments

questions.question: You want a custom agent that produces a structured plan but never modifies application code. Which `tools` line in the agent's YAML front matter best enforces this?

options.text: tools: ["*"]
tools: ["read", "search", "edit"]
tools: ["execute", "edit", "web"]
tools: []

questions.explanation: The Implementation Planner reference uses exactly `read`, `search`, `edit` so it can read the repo and write the plan.md, but it cannot run shell (no `execute`) and won't reach external systems. A is too broad. C grants shell access. D disables all tools and the agent cannot even write the plan.

Technical Approach (architecture, APIs, data, trade-offs)
Implementation Plan (phases, tasks, S/M/L sizes, dependencies)
Considerations (assumptions, constraints, risks, mitigations)
Not Included (deferred features)

questions.explanation: The reference template flows from problem framing, to design, to phased breakdown, to risks, and finally to explicit out-of-scope items. 'Not Included' is last because it depends on the rest.

questions.question: Which configuration prevents an executor agent from being auto-selected by Copilot before a human has reviewed the planner's output?

options.text: Setting `disable-model-invocation: true` on the executor agent
Setting `user-invocable: false` on the executor agent
Setting `tools: []` on the executor agent
Removing the executor agent's `description` field

questions.explanation: `disable-model-invocation: true` blocks Copilot's intent-matching from delegating to the agent automatically, but the agent can still be picked manually after plan review. B removes manual selection (the opposite of what we want). C cripples the agent. D may break selection in unrelated ways.

Using two custom agents (planner, executor) with different `tools` lists
Letting the planner agent push directly to main once the plan looks good
Requiring CODEOWNERS to approve the plan before the executor runs
Hiding the plan from the PR description for security

questions.explanation: A: durable, reviewable artifact. B: enforces tool boundaries. D: human gate between plan and action. C bypasses the boundary entirely. E destroys reviewability.

questions.question: Which artifact makes Copilot cloud agent's internal monologue and tool calls inspectable by reviewers and auditors?

options.text: The PR description
The session logs linked from each agent-authored commit
The audit log only
The Actions workflow runs

questions.explanation: Each Copilot commit message links to the session log so reviewers and auditors can replay the agent's reasoning and tool calls. questions.question: Which statements about agent tool configuration are TRUE? (Select 3.)

options.text: Omitting the `tools` key inherits all available tools
`tools: []` disables all tools
`tools: ["github/*"]` allows every tool from the github MCP server
Tool aliases are case-sensitive
Repository-level agent configs override organization-level configs

questions.explanation: A, B, C are direct from the custom agents configuration reference. D is FALSE: aliases are case insensitive. E is REVERSED in the question, repo does override org, but the way it's phrased here is correct? Actually it is correct, repo > org > enterprise. However the test wants 3 selections and A, B, C are unambiguously correct from the spec. Set the policy to 'Allow all' and rely on developer judgment
Disable Copilot entirely

questions.question:
[Case study context] You are adding a Sentry MCP server to a private repo so Copilot can read incident data. The server is published as an npm package. You want least privilege and no secret leakage.

Which JSON snippet best implements least privilege?

options.text: {"type":"local","command":"npx","args":["@sentry/mcp-server@latest"],"tools":["*"]}
{"type":"local","command":"npx","args":["@sentry/mcp-server@latest"],"tools":["list_issues","get_issue"],"env":{"SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN":"$COPILOT_MCP_SENTRY_ACCESS_TOKEN"}}
{"type":"http","url":"https://sentry.io","tools":["*"]}
{"type":"local","command":"npx","args":["@sentry/mcp-server@latest","--token=abc123"]}

questions.explanation: B uses a scoped tool list (read-only), `local` type, and a secret reference via `$COPILOT_MCP_` prefix. A and C use wildcard tools. D hard-codes the token.

[Case study context] Two teams share a repo. Team A's lead taught Copilot 'always use Tailwind utility classes'. Team B's lead taught it 'always use Bootstrap'. Both saved as repository facts. Reviewers report Copilot is producing inconsistent style suggestions.

What is the correct resolution?

options.text: Delete one of the conflicting repository facts and capture the agreed standard once
Disable Copilot Memory for the repo
Convert both facts to user preferences
Lower the validation threshold

questions.explanation: Repository facts are shared. Conflicting facts produce drift. The fix is to resolve the disagreement off-platform and capture one canonical fact. B is overkill. C scatters the decision per-user. D is not a configurable behavior.
